author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: Zen Buddhism scholar Joan Hiashi is recruited by the State Department to bring her expertise to Havana, ostensibly to convert wealthy Chinese-Cuban businessmen away from Communism, but really as bait: her lover, jazz harpist and telepath Ray Meritan, is suspected of connections to Mercerism, a new religious movement sweeping the world built around 'empathy boxes' — devices that let followers literally share, in real time, the suffering of Wilbur Mercer as he walks toward his death on an alien world.
page_summary:
Zen Buddhism scholar Joan Hiashi is recruited by the State Department to bring her expertise to Havana, ostensibly to convert wealthy Chinese-Cuban businessmen away from Communism, but really as bait: her lover, jazz harpist and telepath Ray Meritan, is suspected of connections to Mercerism, a new religious movement sweeping the world built around 'empathy boxes' — devices that let followers literally share, in real time, the suffering of Wilbur Mercer as he walks toward his death on an alien world. Government officials, unable to determine whether Mercer is human, machine, or extraterrestrial, and unnerved that the movement's technology did not originate on Earth, move to seize and destroy every empathy box in existence while using a Chinese Communist telepath, Mr. Lee, to track Joan and, through her, Meritan. Under coercion, Joan grips an empathy box for the first time and genuinely converts, encountering Mercer directly in a vision where he tells her plainly that there is no salvation, only companionship in suffering — a message that fails to satisfy her interrogators but is real enough to withstand their scrutiny. Bogart Crofts, the State Department official overseeing the operation, cannot resist trying the box himself and is accidentally telepathically fused with Meritan mid-use, learning firsthand what he had spent the story trying to suppress; the experience begins to convert him too, over his superior's furious objection. In the story's final movement, Mercer's organization proves impossible to fully suppress: it begins distributing free cereal-box coupons with instructions for building empathy boxes from ordinary household parts, ensuring the movement survives the government's confiscation campaign by making its technology endlessly, cheaply reproducible.

**Why it matters.** Dick's own account of this story is unusually direct and consequential: he states plainly that he reused its material for Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, and adds the striking judgment that 'the idea is better put forth in the story' than in the novel that made it famous — a rare instance of an author preferring his rough draft to its celebrated expansion. Sutin's bibliographic note adds an important detail: this piece was originally written for the collaborative novel The Ganymede Takeover and cut from the final version, meaning Mercerism's origin is doubly displaced — first excised from one book, then reincorporated wholesale into a different, much more famous one. The story's clearest thematic payoff is Crofts' arc: the official most committed to destroying the movement is also the one who cannot resist testing its claims for himself, and is changed by doing so exactly as Joan was — suggesting the empathy box's power lies not in persuasion but in simple, direct contact, immune to ideological pre-commitment on either side.

*The movement outlasts the government's confiscation campaign not through resistance but through recipe: empathy boxes distributed as buildable instructions hidden in free cereal coupons, ensuring Mercerism survives by becoming a piece of ordinary household technology rather than a controllable object.*

structure.form: novelette in six movements, alternating between Joan/Meritan's story and the government's escalating suppression campaign
movements: Joan's recruitment and Ray Meritan's introduction of the empathy box and Mercerism.
Government officials debate Mercer's true nature (human, machine, or non-terrestrial) and dispatch a Communist telepath, Mr. Lee, to use Joan as a lead.
Joan's arrest in Havana, her first genuine encounter with Mercer through the box, and her conversion.
Meritan's public confession of faith on live television and the government's mass confiscation of empathy boxes.
Bogart Crofts' own accidental use of the box and telepathic fusion with Meritan, and his crisis of loyalty.
The movement's survival strategy: empathy boxes distributed as buildable instructions hidden in free cereal coupons.
structure.point_of_view: alternates among Joan, Ray Meritan, and the government officials (Crofts, Herrick, Mr. Lee), giving the reader access to both the movement's genuine religious content and the state's paranoid, uncomprehending response to it.
structure.central_device: A religious technology (the empathy box) whose central claim — direct, involuntary shared suffering rather than doctrine or belief — cannot be assessed, refuted, or suppressed by any of the political or investigative tools available to the state trying to destroy it.

characters.name: Joan Hiashi
characters.role: Zen Buddhism scholar, State Department recruit
characters.note: Begins the story wishing she and her culture could 'suffer' authentically, and is given exactly that wish, converting to Mercerism the instant she genuinely tries the empathy box rather than merely studying religion from the outside.

characters.name: Ray Meritan
characters.note: Confesses his faith live on television at real professional cost, and remains fundamentally loyal to Joan even once he understands she may have unwittingly enabled his capture.

characters.name: Bogart Crofts
characters.note: The story's most interesting character: rigorously suppresses the movement throughout while visibly, helplessly drawn to try the box himself, and is changed by the one use he permits himself.

characters.name: Mr. Lee
characters.note: Both an antagonist and a genuine believer in his own government's materialist orthodoxy — his reading of Mercerism as mere self-imposed guilt-punishment is presented as a category error rather than cynicism.

characters.name: Wilbur Mercer
characters.role: the figure at the center of the empathy box experience
characters.note: Encountered directly only once, briefly, by Joan — his message is deliberately anti-triumphalist: 'There is no salvation... I am here with you and always will be.'

settings.name: Havana, Cuba
settings.note: A Cold War meeting point where U.S. and Chinese Communist intelligence interests overlap in tracking the same movement, each for different ideological reasons.

settings.name: The empathy-box vision itself
settings.note: A barren, desert landscape where Mercer walks toward his death — rendered with the same weight and reality as the story's ordinary scenes, never marked as 'only' subjective.

motifs: Shared, involuntary suffering as the actual content of religious communion, rather than doctrine, belief, or comfort
A movement's technology (empathy boxes) treated by the state as more dangerous than any belief it carries
Telepathy used as a coercive surveillance tool, ironically producing genuine conversion in the very officials deploying it
A message of explicit non-salvation ('There is no salvation') offered as the movement's central comfort rather than a contradiction of it
Religious technology made unsuppressable through cheap, mass reproducibility — precisely the same mechanism modern totalitarian states use to suppress dissent, turned back against them

distinctive_terms.label: Krishna
distinctive_terms.note: Cited via the Bhagavad Gita in Joan and Mr. Lee's exchange about death and action.

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Dick states directly that this story is the source for Mercerism in Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, and unusually judges the original story's version of the idea superior to the novel's.

evidence.source: Author's story note (The Collected Stories of Philip K. Dick)
evidence.quote: I made use of this story when I wrote my novel DO ANDROIDS DREAM OF ELECTRIC SHEEP? Actually, the idea is better put forth in the story. Here, a religion is regarded as a menace to all political systems; therefore it, too, is a kind of political system
evidence.reading: Direct confirmation of the Mercerism/empathy-box source, and a rare authorial preference for the shorter, earlier version of an idea over its famous novel-length expansion.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: intervention of Wilbur Mercer (left out of the film), who is contacted by gripping "empathy box" handles (cf. "The Little Black Box" [1964] and the empathic Ludens Maze in The Zap Gun).
evidence.reading: Confirms the direct textual link and notes a second reuse of the empathic-device concept in The Zap Gun, worth tracing further.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: "The Little Black Box" (1964), originally part of The Ganymede Takeover but removed from the final version, introduces the empathic
evidence.reading: The story's displaced origin — cut from a collaborative novel before being folded wholesale into Do Androids Dream years later.

evidence.author: Anne R. Dick
evidence.quote: The scary stories "What the Dead Men Say" and "The Little Black Box," and the novel The Unteleported Man, were also part of this output. None of the money from these works
evidence.reading: A first-person account situating the story within a specific, difficult period of Dick's working life and finances.

open_questions: Dick's claim that 'the idea is better put forth in the story' than in Do Androids Dream is a striking authorial self-assessment — is it elaborated anywhere else, or is this the only place he makes the comparison directly?
Sutin references a second reuse of the empathic-device concept in The Zap Gun's 'Ludens Maze' — worth a direct comparison once that novel is covered.

The story's ending (empathy boxes distributed via cereal-box coupons) is a strikingly specific detail — is there a documented real-world inspiration, or a connection to a particular Cold War propaganda/samizdat technique Dick may have had in mind?

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.

later_use: Directly reworked into Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? (1968) as Mercerism and the empathy box; originally intended for the collaborative novel The Ganymede Takeover but removed from the final version, per Sutin.
